gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a split-phase inverter can have a per-leg (L1-N / L2-N) limit at half its rating. EG4's 6000XP manual lists 3,000 W max continuous line wattage against 6,000 W nominal, and a named reviewer writes that the unit cannot shift load between legs, so 4,000 W of 120 V appliances on one leg overloads it even though the house total is under 6 kW.
standout_why: Rival pages read: ecosolarkits.com split-phase explainer (cited) says only that 'some limit how much one leg can carry on its own. Check the manual for a per-leg figure' and gives no figure for any model. Its tip is to keep the legs within roughly 20-30% of each other. ecosolarkits.com EG4 vs Sol-Ark (cited) has total, surge and pass-through figures but nothing on legs or imbalance. liveoffthegrid.com/specs/inverters (cited) only labels units '120/240 split-phase'. eg4electronics.com FlexBOSS21 page (cited) gives 12000VA and 50A nominal but no per-leg or imbalance spec. sol-ark.com 15K page gives 15 kW grid, 13 kW backup, 24 kW surge and 200 A pass-through, with no per-leg figure. None of them puts a per-leg number on a named model.
decides: This mostly affects ChatGPT's budget pick, the EG4 6000XP ('6 kW continuous, 120/240V'). In practice that rating means 3 kW per 120 V leg, and the legs don't balance each other. A shopper with mostly 120 V loads (fridge, sump pump, microwave, space heater) has to split them evenly across L1 and L2 or buy a larger or second unit. That confirms the 6000XP only for 240 V-heavy or carefully balanced off-grid panels. For the FlexBOSS21 and Sol-Ark 15K I could not open a maker per-leg figure, so the page should tell shoppers to check that line in the manual before moving 120 V circuits into a backup subpanel.

findings.label: Max continuous line (per-leg) wattage vs nominal output
findings.value: 3,000 W per line; 6,000 W nominal; 120/240 VAC output
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP User Manual v1.2 (©2024 EG4 Electronics), p.5 Technical Specifications, ManualsLib copy
findings.note: Text extracted from the AC output block lists the labels 'MAX CONT. LINE WATTAGE' and then 'NOMINAL POWER OUTPUT', followed in the same order by the values '3000W' and '6000W'. The extraction did not keep labels and values side by side, so I matched them by order. The SolarTech review below gives the same 3,000 W figure. EG4's own PDF (eg4electronics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/EG4-6000XP-Manual.pdf) would not render as text.

findings.label: Load balancing between legs
findings.value: None: 3,000 W max per 120 V leg, and each leg runs on its own
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP Complete Guide: Specs, Installation, and Real-World Performance (2025), Jonathan Richter, SolarTech, 2025-08-11
findings.note: Richter writes: 'Per-leg limitation: 3000W maximum per 120V leg', 'the 6000XP cannot automatically balance loads between legs', and 'If you have 4000W of appliances on one 120V leg, the inverter will overload even though the total system load is well under 6000W.' The article's citations don't cover this claim, so the manual line above is the primary source.
